paragraphs.heading: What a sea cliff is
paragraphs.text: A sea cliff is a steep slope cut by sea waves. A coast shaped this way is called a cliffed coast, or an abrasion coast, and it contrasts with a flat or alluvial coast. Its cliffs are steep but may or may not be precipitous. Such cliffs can arise where the land surface dips at a fairly steep angle below the water table. The unbroken action of waves on the coastline there, known as abrasion, may create the steep drop. How steep the slope ends up depends on several things, including the jointing, bedding and hardness of the cliff's materials and the erosion processes themselves.

paragraphs.heading: How a cliff moves inland
paragraphs.text: The slope is constantly being eroded. Waves attack the foot of the cliff and, by constant abrasion, cut a hollow called a wave-cut notch, which leaves an overhang above it. As the cliff is undercut the overhang grows, until it collapses under its own weight. The sea gradually carries the broken debris away from the area in front of the cliff. As the cliffs collapse, the shoreline moves back inland.

paragraphs.heading: How fast it happens
paragraphs.text: The speed of this retreat depends in particular on how strong the surf is, how high the cliff is, how often storm surges come, and how hard the bedrock is. The Mecklenburg coast in Germany moves back by about 25 centimetres a year. The chalk cliffs of southern England retreat by only half a centimetre a year.

paragraphs.heading: What forms in front of the cliff
paragraphs.text: Cliffed coasts can be made of loose material, as at the Red Cliff on Sylt, a German island, or of hard rock, like the red sandstone cliffs on Heligoland. Where the rock resists erosion relatively well, as sandstone, limestone or granite do, a flat rocky shelf forms in front of the cliff. It is called a wave-cut platform or abrasion platform, and it is the cliff's foot, preserved at the level of the water table and below it. Where the material is only fairly or hardly resistant, a beach forms in front of the cliff instead. If the coast is lifted by tectonic uplift, these platforms can be raised to become coastal terraces.

paragraphs.heading: Arches and stacks
paragraphs.text: On a rocky cliffed coast, waves may carve notches into both sides of a promontory at a narrow point, and a natural arch may form. As the coastline recedes further the arch collapses, and a stack is left standing on the wave-cut platform. Old Harry Rocks in Dorset are a prominent example in England, and the Lange Anna on Heligoland is the best-known one in Germany. Waves are not the only force driving the retreat of a rocky cliffed coast. General weathering of the bedrock is almost equally important.

paragraphs.heading: Living cliffs and dead cliffs
paragraphs.text: A living cliff is one on a coast that is still active: it is being eroded and is receding. A dead cliff is reached only by very high waves, and so changes very little. A clear sign of a dead cliff is a cover of vegetation, which appears as wave action against it subsides. A good example of a dead cliff is the Königsstuhl on the island of Rügen. Others stand a few kilometres inland in the regions of today's Wadden Sea coast of the North Sea. They show the former coastline, which the sea left as the water level in the North Sea fell.
